findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and render identities share denials
findings.body:
The denial key is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and parent folder. The identity type is not part of it.

Anonymous (`anonymous:0`) and the render service (`render:0`) both parse to UserUID "0", so they get the same denial key. If an anonymous Check on a dashboard is denied, the entry is cached for 30s. A following `render:0` Check for `dashboards:read` on that dashboard then hits the denial cache and is refused, even though the renderer is meant to be granted read on everything. Image rendering breaks for that window.

The reverse also happens. The renderer is denied every non-read action, so a renderer denial can block an anonymous identity whose configured role (e.g. Editor) should allow the action.

Fix: include the identity type in the denial key (and ideally the resolved user UID), or skip the denial cache for render/anonymous.

findings.title: Ambiguous '_' delimiter in denial cache key lets different resources collide
findings.body:
`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins userUID, action, name and parent with "_". Grafana dashboard and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so different requests can produce the same key.

Example: dashboard `a_b` in folder `c` and dashboard `a` in folder `b_c` both map to `<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one makes Check return `Allowed:false` for the other for up to 30s, without ever looking at the user's permissions.

The key also reuses the `.perm_` prefix of `userPermCacheKey`, which mixes two value types (bool vs map) in the same key space.

Fix: use a distinct prefix and an unambiguous encoding, such as a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, length-prefixing, or hashing the tuple.

findings.title: Every denied check on a new resource now forces a full DB permission fetch
findings.body:
Before this change, a cached permission set answered Check entirely from cache. Now, when the cached set does not allow the request, Check always calls `getIdentityPermissions`. That path no longer consults `permCache` and re-runs the permission store query, plus basic-role and team lookups once those 30s caches expire.

The denial cache only short-circuits repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, folder) tuple. So each distinct resource a user cannot access costs one DB round trip, and singleflight only merges concurrent calls.

For anonymous access (one shared permission set for all anonymous users), requests for many distinct or random dashboard UIDs each trigger a DB query and each add a new denial-cache entry. That is a cheap load-amplification path compared to before.

Possible mitigations: rate-limit or bound the fallback, e.g. only re-query if the cached perms are older than some threshold, or refresh once per user/action rather than per resource.

findings.title: Denial-cache test seeds a non-granting permission, so it passes without the denial cache
findings.body:
The test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says it sets an allowing permission "to prove this is not checked". It actually stores `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` treats a false value as not granted.

Without the denial cache, the flow would be: cached perms deny, the DB fallback runs, the default `fakeStore` returns no permissions, and the result is deny. So the test passes whether or not the denial cache works.

The value should be `true`, so the cached perms would allow access and only the denial entry can produce `Allowed:false`.

There is also no test that a denial is written to `permDenialCache` after a DB-backed deny, and none for the collision cases above.
